Unit the data comes out, we won't know what this money actually produces in terms of arrests, deportations, and detention bed-days. This is what we call an  accountability gap, where funding gets appropriated and the enforcement record comes later.

To put the scale in perspective: NILC describes this as roughly the equivalent of eight years of DHS funding, passed all at once, with no meaningful accountability measures attached. And House appropriators are already working on additional ICE funding for FY 2027.

Section 202(9) doesn't require a conviction or even a sustained charge. It covers people who were charged with unauthorized entry and had charges dropped, and even those flagged by ICE after almost any arrest.
Section 202(9) gives ICE $350 million specifically to conduct enforcement in cities or states DHS designates as "non-cooperating" with federal immigration policy.

The bill bypassed the normal annual appropriations process through budget reconciliation. That's significant because the regular process included oversight requirements, detention transparency rules, and civil rights protections. This law includes none of those.
Congress just passed S.2, which sends nearly $70 billion in new funding to ICE and CBP for mass deportation and detention, that's $38 billion to ICE alone.
